prize_parts.citation: For showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, creating the theory of credit cycles.

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from B012 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) to B002 (Kiyotaki and Moore). This is a close call, and I do not think it reverses the merit ranking. B002 and B012 are near-equal on originality, maturity (both about three decades) and reach. What moved me is exact credit and the one open evidential question I raised in round 1. On credit, Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is a two-author originating paper, and a two-name award omits nobody who wrote it. For B012, the exchange showed that no three-name set is fully defensible. Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes is the demand-side core, but Bresnahan, Benkard and Levin, and Reiss are real omissions. Teorell's Pakes-alone variant shows the cost of fixing that by cutting further. Citation wording cannot repair this, because the issue is who is credited, not how the work is described. On evidence, I had weighed the weaker identification of collateral amplification against B002. The chair asked what would count as evidence. My recollection, which I have not verified, is that micro-level studies of firms and households exploit variation in collateral values, such as real-estate prices, to identify effects on borrowing and investment. That evidence supports the existence of the channel, not the size of aggregate amplification. A mechanism supported by this kind of design looks less like pure theory than I implied in round 1. Its post-2008 policy use and its absorption into quantitative macro give it breadth beyond one subfield. I apply the same criteria as before: a clear origin, durable use, years of confirmation, and an economic framework that gives the result meaning. Kiyotaki-Moore meets them with cleaner credit than B012 can.
statement.case_against: My move rests partly on attribution, which is a presentation criterion as much as a merit one. The merit comparison with B012 is not settled in B002's favour. The strongest reservation is that the size of collateral-driven amplification in the aggregate is weakly identified, and the micro evidence I rely on is unverified recollection that speaks to the channel, not to the magnitude. Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is a real risk. If the Committee reads credit cycles as already honoured, B002 loses ground. Limiting the award to two names leaves out the Gertler and Gilchrist accelerator strand, which several members regard as part of the same literature. Finally, B012 has an established record of changing practice in merger review, antitrust and applied fields. A committee that weights measurement frameworks as heavily as mechanisms could reasonably still put B012 first, and my own round-1 view was that way.

responses.point: Teorell proposes two parts: Kiyotaki and Moore for B002, and Pakes alone for B012, under the three-person cap. He records that omitting Berry and Levinsohn is a real attribution loss and that the two parts share no obvious theme.
responses.response: I considered this pairing seriously, since it combines my fallback with his. I do not support it. Pakes alone separates him from the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes demand-side core. As I argued in round 1, that core is the compact, well-identified centre of the B012 contribution. Teorell himself calls the omission a real loss that he accepts only because the cap binds. The pairing also has no shared achievement, so the Committee would be combining two unrelated results mainly to use the cap. I read the cap as a reason to prefer a single part whose credit is cleaner, not as a reason to thin the credit on a second part. That is a large part of why I moved to B002 alone.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers adding Gertler to Kiyotaki and Moore as the quantitative financial-frictions strand. He accepts the two-name version as a fallback, and he argues that Gertler's later intermediary work with Kiyotaki and Karadi is separable from the 2022 recognition.
responses.response: I accept the two-name fallback and rank it above the three-name version. On the chair's question about evidence separating Gertler's intermediary work from the 2022 prize, I cannot answer from the supplied materials, and I will not guess. That is itself a reason not to include him. A citation that depends on an unresolved credit judgment, with Gertler also named under B043, is less defensible than one that does not. If the Committee wanted a broader financial-frictions citation, I would need a clearer account of what Gertler specifically established that the 1997 paper did not. Absent that, I keep the part to Kiyotaki and Moore.

responses.point: Boppart argues that the 2022 prize on banks, runs and intermediation concerns a different mechanism from Kiyotaki-Moore's collateral and asset-price feedback. He treats the overlap as thematic and not a duplication of the discovery, and he accepts that B002 would be the candidate to lose if the Committee judged the area saturated.
responses.response: I agree that the mechanisms differ, and this contributed to my move. The 2022 work concerns the role of banks and runs in financial crises, whereas the 1997 paper concerns how borrower collateral values feed back on credit and asset prices. In answer to the chair's question on prize overlap, the principle I apply is that adjacency to a recent prize is a timing and balance consideration for the Committee, not a measure of scientific merit. I would apply it to the other candidates in the same way: 2008 for B025, 2024 for B050 and B021. Treating it as a merit demerit for B002 but not elsewhere would be inconsistent. I still count it as a real risk for the vote, as you do.

responses.point: Andersson prefers B012 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) first. He regards BLP as the clear centre of demand estimation, notes that the three-name limit omits Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, and says Rubinstein-Wolinsky is a distinct contribution if B001 is considered.
responses.response: Andersson and I reached the same view on the BLP core, and I left B012 as my first alternative because of that. Where my view changed is on the cost of the omissions. He treats them as an acceptable cost of the cap. I now think they are a defect that wording cannot fix, because Bresnahan, Benkard and Levin are credited on the same ballot, and he himself says Benkard and Levin belong to the dynamic-game strand that a demand-focused citation misses. By contrast, a two-name B002 has no comparable omission from the originating paper. I do not claim this makes B012 less meritorious. If the Committee decides the omissions are tolerable, I would still support Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn as the three-name set.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B012 first. He argues that BLP is both a method and a discovery, and that the cap is a constraint every multi-contributor shortlisted candidate faces, with B043 facing it much more severely.
responses.response: I made the same method-and-discovery argument in round 1 and have not abandoned it, so my change does not depend on resolving it. I agree that the cap binds on B043 much more than on B012. But the comparison that matters here is between B012 and B002, where the cap binds very differently. It forces an omission from B012, but it leaves out nobody from the 1997 paper. Strömberg's point that three decades of critique without displacement is a sign of maturity is persuasive and applies equally to B002 on the theory side. I take the real difference between us to be how heavily to weigh attribution against the breadth of downstream use.

uncertainties: Whether the micro evidence on collateral values and investment that I recall is as strong and well-identified as I think. It is not independently verified, and it speaks to the channel more than to aggregate magnitude.
How much of the credit-cycle mechanism the Committee regards as already covered by the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
Whether my move from B012 to B002 reflects a real difference in merit or only the cleaner attribution of the two-name award. I think the merit comparison is close, and I hold it loosely.

Whether the omission of Bresnahan, Benkard and Levin is tolerable under a Pakes-Berry-Levinsohn citation, which decides whether B012 should rank above B002 for a Committee that weights measurement frameworks heavily.
Whether leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist makes the B002 citation look narrower than the accelerator literature. I cannot verify how that literature divides credit.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the preferred part (B002) or the alternatives (B012 and B025). My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited names on any shortlisted ballot, and my own field of labour economics and the economics of crime is not adjacent to macro-finance. I move from B012 in round 1 to B002 in round 2 with no personal connection to either. My AER editorial board role is not candidate-specific. I disclose this without adjudicating it.
